newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Shevardnadze to decide fate of Security Minister.
newsitem.headline: Shevardnadze to decide fate of Security Minister.

text.p: Georgia's parliament set aside a drive to impeach the country's embattled security minister on Friday and left his fate in the hands of President Eduard Shevardnadze.
A group of lawmakers agreed to hand over evidence they claim to have collected against Shota Kviraya to Shevardnadze, who can then decide whether to leave him in his post or sack him.

The deputies accuse Kviraya of personally executing six suspected marauders during a 1993 civil war, authorising the bugging of telephones of several journalists and working for Russian intelligence services.
Kviraya vigorously denied the charges in a letter published in one of Georgia's leading newspapers this week.

The deputies, led by Irina Sarishvili-Chanturia, leader of the centre-right National Independence Party, said they abandoned their impeachment bid at the request of members of Shevardnadze's centrist Citizens' Union, which has a majority in parliament.
But they said Shevardnadze must take speedy action or they would re-start the impeachment process.

"We hope at least this time that the president will take a principled decision to replace not only the minister, but all those who occupy government posts at the dictate of Russia," Sarishvili-Chanturia told reporters.
Relations between Moscow and the former Soviet republic have been frosty since Georgia accused Russia of backing separatists in the breakaway region of Abkhazia during the civil war.
"If the president does not take a speedy decision, then we will collect the necessary signatures (for impeachment) and send our request to the Supreme Court," Sarishvili-Chanturia said.
Shevardnadze said earlier this week that Kviraya should be removed from office if some of the charges against him were true.

The deputies say they acted to remove Kviraya now because of the threat of renewed fighting with separatists in Abkhazia. They say the country needs a "cleaner" security apparatus in the event of war.

Talks with the Abkhaz have not brought peace and only a month remains before a deadline set by Georgia for Russian peacekeeping troops to start leaving the region unless they agree to do more to resettle Georgian refugees and patrol more Abkhaz territory. So far they have refused.

The head of a parliamentary investigation commission says video footage exists showing Kviraya, then interior minister, of personally killing six alleged looters with a pistol in the western city of Zugdidi near the end of the civil war in 1993. The footage was not immediately available to journalists.

Sarishvili-Chanturia said Kviraya told a closed parliamentary session on Thursday that he authorised phone taps of several leading journalists. "He said that in some cases the telephone eavesdropping had been legal," she said.
But she added that Kviraya claimed not to have authorised some of the bugging and said the responsible members of the security apparatus had been dismissed.
